title: ANOVA F-Ratio Visualiser
summary: Control the separation, spread and size of three simulated groups, and watch F respond to both halves of its fraction. Then meet three different patterns of means that all produce the same F.
learningObjectives: Describe F as the ratio of the between-groups mean square to the within-groups mean square.
Predict what happens to F when group means separate, when within-group variability grows and when the sample gets larger.
Explain why a large F is not a measure of how large a difference between groups is.
State what a significant omnibus test does and does not license about particular groups.
Explain why post-hoc comparisons answer a different question from the omnibus test.
interactionTypes: live simulation with a real analysis of generated data
strip plot with drawn between-groups reach
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every score is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, a number input, radio groups, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; every slider announces a meaningful value such as 'population means 44.0, 52.0 and 60.0'. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - group n, mean and SD for the strip plot, and each group's distance from the grand mean for the pattern picture - and a disclosure holds the full source table of sums of squares, degrees of freedom and mean squares. Group means are drawn as heavy bars and printed as numbers beneath each column, and the grand mean is a labelled dashed line, so nothing is carried by colour alone. Experiment 1 keeps one pinned primary result measured at 510px tall at 1366x768 and Experiment 2 at 392px, so the controls beside them stay usable above the fold. Every preset and resample announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to each experiment's heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: F is a fraction: move the signal, move the noise, and meet three patterns of means that share one F
simulationNotes: Experiment 1 draws n observations per group from Normal(52 - s, sigma), Normal(52, sigma) and Normal(52 + s, sigma), where s and sigma are set by sliders, and then runs an actual one-way ANOVA on the generated sample rather than reporting population values: SS between is the sum over groups of n times the squared distance of the group mean from the grand mean, SS within is the pooled sum of squared deviations from each group's own mean, and F is their ratio of mean squares. Tail areas come from the regularised incomplete beta function, evaluated by continued fraction with a Lanczos log-gamma, so p is exact to display precision rather than looked up. The groups are labelled A, B and C on purpose, so that no story about revision does the explaining. Doubling sigma divides the amount by which F exceeds 1 by four, because E[MS between] is sigma squared plus n times the sum of squared population deviations over k minus 1, while E[MS within] is sigma squared; the page states this exactly rather than claiming F itself quarters. Experiment 2 uses three sets of three means - 49/52/55, 50/50/55.196 and 46.804/52/52 - constructed to have identical sums of squared deviations from their own grand means, so at 30 per group and a within-group SD of 6 all three give SS between 540.0 and F(2, 87) = 7.50, p = .001. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study, participant, revision method or dataset is involved.
